data.text:
Your T2202 tuition slip is worth real money at tax time. The question is: whose money?

The rule (federal, 2026): the tuition credit is 14% of eligible tuition shown on your T2202, if you paid that school more than $100 in the year.
Example: $8,000 of tuition = a $1,120 federal credit.

Step 1: the student claims it first. It must bring the student's own tax to zero. With $12,000 from a summer job, a student already owes no federal tax, so none of the credit is needed that year.
Step 2: transfer. Up to $5,000 of this year's tuition can go to ONE person: a parent, a grandparent, or a spouse/common-law partner. That's $700 off their tax (5,000 × 14%), and only if they owe tax.
Step 3: carry forward. The other $3,000 stays with the student, with no expiry: a $420 credit, but only on the student's own future return. Carried-forward amounts can't be transferred later.

And the federal education and textbook amounts ended after 2016. Tuition is what's left.

data.text:
A CRA notice says you owe $5,000. Before you pay, or panic, check three usual suspects.

Suspect 1: a forgotten slip. CRA matches slips (T4, T5…). Example: $15,000 of T5 interest never reported, taxed at about 33.25% (20.5% federal + 12.75% Manitoba at an ~$80K income) = $4,988, nearly the whole bill. CRA can generally reassess within 3 years of the original notice.
Suspect 2: a payment applied to another year. Your CRA My Account shows how each payment was applied.
Suspect 3: instalments. If your net tax owing was over $3,000 this year and in one of the two previous years, CRA expected payments during the year, and charges interest on late ones.

The twist: you have time. CRA can't start legal collection for 90 days after the notice, and you can object until the later of 90 days after the notice or one year after the filing deadline. But interest compounds daily from April 30, even while you sort it out.

Action: open the notice, read the explanation of changes, match every slip in My Account, then pay or object before the deadline.

Can't pay your tax bill, so you don't file? That's the move that costs extra. Three returns, same deadline:

tiktokData.title: Incorporate and Keep $6,000 More? It's Not Lower Tax (Canada)

data.text:
Same $100,000 of profit. Incorporate, and you keep about $6,000 more. But not from lower tax.

Option 1, sole proprietor (Manitoba 2026, single): income tax $21,729 + CPP $9,293 → you keep $68,978.
Option 2, a corporation paying it all out as dividends: 9% corporate tax ($9,000) + personal tax on $91,000 of dividends ($16,014) = $25,014 of income tax, $3,285 MORE than the sole proprietor. You keep $74,986.

Where does the $6,008 come from? Dividends skip CPP: no contributions, but no CPP pension built, and dividends create no RRSP room.

The real edge: money you leave inside. Leave $40,000 in the company and so far it has only been taxed at 9%; personal tax comes when you take it out (a deferral, not a discount).

A corporation also files its own tax return (T2) every year. Run your own numbers with an accountant first.

Years later, Sam withdraws the $10,000. At Sam's lower income, the tax at today's rates is about $2,480 (24.8%). Roughly $1,500 less.

The trap: if Sam withdraws while Alex contributed to a spousal RRSP this year or in the two years before, the withdrawal is taxed to Alex: about $4,340 (ITA 146(8.3)).
The twist: the rule counts calendar years. One deposit in December 2026 keeps 2026, 2027 and 2028 locked; 2029 is clear.

Time withdrawals around the last contribution, and check with an accountant before taking money out.
